meaning: Name of a fabulous mountain — the central point of Jambūdvīpa, round which the sun, moon and planets revolve; the Olympus of Hindu mythology and abode of the gods.

phonemes.desc: Short e as in “set”; the name is pre-Vedic in feel, its etymology uncertain.
Long ū as in “rule”; the name closes on the resonant liquid.
The axis mountain — the Olympus of Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain cosmology alike.

kin.label: Jain

pronunciation.note: All three Indian religions share Meru — the one mountain in the centre of every map.

domains.title: The Axis Mountain, Olympus of the Hindus
domains.subtitle: The Centre of the World
domains.lead: Meru is the world’s axle: the golden mountain at the centre of the cosmos, around which the sun, moon, and planets revolve, on whose summit Indra’s city stands, and whose four faces of gold, crystal, ruby, and lapis feed the four great rivers of the directions. Every Indian cosmology — Hindu, Buddhist, Jain — puts Meru in the middle; every mandala is its plan.

cards.name: The Axis
cards.desc: The world turns on Meru; the pole star wheels above its summit as the heavens’ nail-head.

cards.name: The Four Faces
cards.desc: Gold to the east, crystal south, ruby west, lapis north — the four colours of the mandala.

cards.name: City of the Gods
cards.desc: Indra’s Amarāvatī crowns the summit; the thirty-three gods feast in its halls.

cards.name: The Mandala’s Map
cards.desc: Every maṇḍala diagrams Meru: centre, four gates, and the enclosing world-rings.

mythology.lead: Meru’s mythology is cosmography — the mountain’s biography is the world’s architecture. It rises from the centre of Jambudvīpa, the rose-apple continent; the sun’s chariot circles it daily; the Ganges falls first on its summit and only then to the earth; and the gods’ wars are fought on its terraces. The Purāṇic geographies measure all distance from its base.

myths.title: The Mountain of Measure
myths.text: The Purāṇas give Meru its statistics: 84,000 leagues high, its base 32,000 across, its summit the square of the gods’ city. The sun’s horses, tired from circling it, rest at night on its western face; the moon’s waxing is the gods’ drinking of the lunar soma on its terraces. The mountain is the cosmos’s clock, scale, and sceptre.

myths.title: The River’s First Fall
myths.text: When Bhagīratha won the Ganges’ descent for his burned ancestors, the river fell first from heaven onto the matted hair of Śiva — and before that, the tradition adds, upon Meru’s summit, where the gods’ gardens divided her into the seven streams. Meru is the river’s first landing, heaven’s customs-house.

myths.title: The Mountain Diagrammed
myths.text: The Buddhist and Hindu maṇḍala is Meru flattened into a map: the square’s four gates are its faces, the inner palace the summit’s city, the concentric rings its seven world-encircling ranges. To construct a mandala is to rebuild Meru; to enter it is to climb. The Vajrayāna made the diagram the path itself.

myths.title: The Churning’s Spindle
myths.text: When the gods and demons churned the ocean of milk, the churning-rod was Mandara, Meru’s little brother of a mountain; the serpent Vāsuki the rope. Meru’s family thus supplied the axis of the gods’ greatest work — the axis-mountain’s line, lending itself to every cosmic rotation.

lore.syncretism: Meru is shared property: Hindu Meru, Buddhist Sumeru, Jain Meru of the madhyaloka. The Greeks of Bactria heard Olympus in it; and the East Asian Buddhist cosmologies drew Sumeru as the world’s spike on temple banners from Java to Japan. The mountain out-religioned every religion that mapped it.
lore.culturalLegacy: Every mandala, stupa, and temple plan is a Meru; the prayer-wheel’s axis and the pagoda’s spire are its hardware. ‘Sumeru’ and ‘Meru’ entered the names of a thousand monasteries and mountains — and travellers to the real Himalaya argued for centuries which peak the geographers had meant.
lore.extendedMeditation: Meru: the name of the centre, restored at the centre of a plain line of letters. It needs no diacritic — the mountain carries its own height, and every reader’s eye climbs it. Two syllables, eighty-four thousand leagues.
lore.archaeology: Meru’s monuments are every stupa and pagoda — the Borobudur terraces walk the pilgrim up Sumeru; the temple mountains of Angkor are Meru in sandstone. The maṇḍala-paintings of Tibet diagram it ten thousand times.
lore.cult: No separate cult — every cosmological rite is his. The consecration of a stupa ‘plants Meru’; the temple’s foundation deposits place the mountain under the god’s throne. The circumambulation of any sacred centre is its summit-walk.
lore.iconography: The stepped pyramid-mountain, four-faced and jewel-coloured, crowned by Indra’s palace or the thousand-armed deity; or the square mandala with its four gates. The stupa’s harmikā tower is Meru’s tip in portable form.
lore.reception: History of science studies Meru as the ancient world’s most influential cosmic model — the flat-earth cosmography’s greatest rival, and the template of every Asian sacred building. The pagoda’s archaeology is, in one reading, nothing but Meru’s long migration east.
